Worked example: Harvest Lane. Tolu's task: sending tomorrow's delivery list to the rider. It happens six evenings a week.

Trigger: 6 p.m. on a delivery day. Outcome: the rider has a complete list of tomorrow's paid orders before 7 p.m. and has replied "OK".

  1. Open the Orders notebook. (notebook)
  2. Find every order for tomorrow's date. (notebook)
  3. Check each order is paid. (bank app)
  4. Copy name, phone, address and items for each paid order. (notebook, WhatsApp Business)
  5. Group the orders by area: Bodija, Mokola, Ring Road. (WhatsApp Business)
  6. Send the list to the rider. (WhatsApp Business)
  7. Confirm the rider replied "OK". (WhatsApp Business)

FRIED: F yes (six times a week). R yes (a new hire could follow the steps above). I mostly: orders are in a notebook today, so this becomes fully digital only once orders live in a sheet. E yes (a missed address means a failed delivery and a refund). D yes. Four and a half of five: a strong candidate.

Note: step 5 is really route planning, which needs local judgement. Keep that one with Tolu and automate the rest.
mistakes: Steps that hide several actions, such as "sort out the orders", instead of one verb + object each.
Naming the first action as the trigger ("open the notebook") instead of the event that starts it (6 p.m., a new message).
Writing the outcome as an activity ("list sent") rather than the result someone cares about (rider has a complete, paid-only list).
Giving a FRIED total with no yes or no per letter, or ticking F for a task that only happens monthly.
b.pass: Five to ten numbered steps, each a single verb + object, with the trigger, outcome and the tool used at every step labelled, and a yes or no for each FRIED letter. A classmate could do the task from the list without asking a question.
b.redo: Send it back if steps are vague or bundled, the trigger or outcome is missing, or FRIED is scored as a number with no reasoning per letter.

Worked example: a fictional private school in Abeokuta, fee payments. Interview: the bursar, 40 minutes.

Lanes: Parent · Bursar · Class teacher.

  1. Parent: pays fees by transfer, sends a screenshot to the bursar's WhatsApp. Handoff 1 (screenshots get buried in chats).
  2. Bursar: finds the screenshot, checks the bank statement. Decision: amount matches? No → message parent. Yes → continue.
  3. Bursar: writes a receipt in the receipt book, photographs it, sends it to the parent.
  4. Bursar: updates the paper "cleared" list on Friday. Handoff 2 (teachers get it late, so cleared pupils are wrongly turned away).
  5. Teacher: lets cleared pupils sit exams.

Scores (fee season, per week):

StepRuns/wkMinErrorDiff.Priority
Match screenshot to statement803High ×2Medium ÷2240
Write and send receipt802Med ×1.5Easy ÷1240
Update cleared list160High ×2Easy ÷1120
Chase unpaid parents303Med ×1.5Hard ÷345

The case. The first automation is payment confirmation: parents pay through a payment link that signals when money lands, the pupil's row in a Fees sheet changes to Paid, a receipt goes out automatically, and teachers see a live view-only cleared list. Receipts depend on confirmation, so the two top steps are built together. This saves about 460 minutes (7.7 hours) a week in fee season, worth about ₦66,000 a month at ₦2,000 an hour (7.7 × 2,000 × 4.3). Tools start on free plans at this volume; if building takes 15 hours, it pays back within about two weeks. Kept manual: chasing unpaid parents and agreeing payment plans. Drawing lanes but not circling handoffs, or putting yes/no questions in ordinary boxes instead of diamonds.
A payback estimate with no hourly value or no weekly-to-monthly conversion (× 4.3).
Automating the relationship step (chasing debts, negotiating) instead of keeping it human and preparing the facts for it.

Worked example: Harvest Lane's payment webhook, order HL-0042. All three POSTs go to the same webhook.site URL with Content-Type: application/json.

# Test 1: normal order, plus a custom header
X-Source: harvest-lane-test
{ "event": "payment.success", "order_id": "HL-0042",
  "amount_kobo": 1250000, "customer_phone": "+2348030000000",
  "paid_at": "2026-10-01T09:12:04+01:00" }

# Test 2: customer_phone removed
{ "event": "payment.success", "order_id": "HL-0042",
  "amount_kobo": 1250000, "paid_at": "2026-10-01T09:12:04+01:00" }

# Test 3: amount as text
{ "event": "payment.success", "order_id": "HL-0042",
  "amount_kobo": "12500", "customer_phone": "+2348030000000",
  "paid_at": "2026-10-01T09:12:04+01:00" }

What the receiver saw: all three arrived and were recorded, including the X-Source header in the headers list. webhook.site accepts anything. That is the lesson: checking is our job.

Checklist before trusting a payment webhook:

  1. Required fields exist (event, order_id, amount_kobo). Test 2: phone missing. We can still mark the order paid, but we flag it so nobody sends a receipt to a blank number.
  2. Types are right. Test 3: "12500" is text, so reject it.
  3. Amount matches the order. HL-0042 totals ₦12,500 = 1,250,000 kobo. Test 1 matches. Test 3 would be ₦125 even as a number, so it fails twice.
  4. The event is expected. Only payment.success marks an order paid (Test 1).
  5. Not already processed. Sending Test 1 twice produced two identical requests, so check order_id before updating.
  6. It really came from the provider. Our X-Source header arrived exactly as typed, which proves anyone can send any header. Real providers sign webhooks; we verify the signature (Module 2.5).
mistakes: Forgetting the Content-Type: application/json header, so the body arrives as unreadable text.
Writing a checklist that isn't linked to any test they actually sent.
Treating a custom header like X-Source as proof of who sent the request.
Checking the amount in naira against a kobo value, or using a real customer's phone number in the test.
s.pass: Evidence of three POSTs (normal, missing phone, amount as text) and the custom header visible on the receiving side, plus a checklist of at least four checks, each tied to a named test.
s.redo: Send it back if fewer than three tests were sent, the header can't be found, checks aren't linked to tests, or real customer data was used.

Worked example: Harvest Lane's rain alert bot. Token and chat_id below are placeholders; never show your real token.

1. Find the chat_id (after messaging the bot once):

GET https://api.telegram.org/bot<YOUR_TOKEN>/getUpdates

# The chat id sits at: result[0].message.chat.id  e.g. 123456789

2. Send tomorrow's rain decision:

POST https://api.telegram.org/bot<YOUR_TOKEN>/sendMessage
Content-Type: application/json

{ "chat_id": 123456789, "text": "Rain chance tomorrow: 70%. Pack covers." }

Status 200 and "ok": true in the response; the message appears on your phone. The 70 comes from daily.precipitation_probability_max[1] in the 0.2 solved problem, and 70 is at least 50, so the text says "Pack covers."

3. Paystack request, written only:

POST https://api.paystack.co/transaction/initialize
Authorization: Bearer <SECRET_KEY>
Content-Type: application/json

{ "email": "customer@example.com", "amount": 1250000 }

₦12,500 × 100 = 1,250,000 kobo. POST because it creates a transaction. The key goes in the Authorization header with the Bearer prefix. While learning it would be a test key (sk_test_…), never a live one.

Why each part:

  • getUpdates is a GET because it only reads. The body is an object whose result key holds a list of updates, so the first message is result[0].
  • sendMessage is a POST because it sends something new. The body is JSON, so the Content-Type header must say so, or Telegram won't read chat_id.
  • The bot token sits inside the URL path, which makes it easy to leak in a screenshot of the address bar. If it ever shows, revoke it in @BotFather and use the new one.

Submit: a phone screenshot of the bot's message, a Hoppscotch screenshot with status 200 and the token hidden, and the written Paystack request.
mistakes: Calling getUpdates before messaging the bot, so the result list is empty and there is no chat_id.
Writing the Paystack amount as 12500 (naira) instead of 1250000 (kobo).
Leaving out the Bearer prefix, or showing the bot token or a secret key in a screenshot.
Sending the Paystack request with a live key instead of only writing it out.
g.pass: A phone screenshot showing the bot's rain message, and a written Paystack request with POST, the initialize URL, Authorization: Bearer and Content-Type headers, and amount 1250000.
g.redo: Send it back if no message reached the phone, the amount is in naira, a header is missing, or any token or secret key is visible.

Worked example: Tolu describes herself and Harvest Lane. (Phone is a sample number.)

{
  "name": "Tolu",
  "city": "Ibadan",
  "phone": "+2348000000000",
  "orders_per_day": 45,
  "delivers_on_sunday": false,
  "website": null,

Paths checked in the lab:

  • business.name → "Harvest Lane" (string)
  • products[2] → "onions" (string; third item, counted from 0)
  • business.riders → 4 (number)

Why these types: the phone is a string so the country code and every digit are kept exactly; nobody will ever add two phone numbers together. orders_per_day is a number because it will be used in sums. delivers_on_sunday is a real boolean, not the text "no". The website is null on purpose: we know there isn't one, which is different from forgetting to fill it in.

Using single quotes or leaving a trailing comma after the last field.
Writing products[3] for the third item instead of products[2].
Using an empty string "" where null was meant, so one of the six features is missing.

Screenshots of the five sheets (Price_List, Customers, Pending, Orders, Conversation_Log) after the test run, with made-up customer data.
Exported JSON of the bot workflow, SUB · Price an order and the daily report workflow, with no keys or tokens pasted into fields.
Telegram screenshots of conversations 2, 3, 8, 12 and 13 (summary with buttons, confirmation, injection attempt, double tap, stock race).
The 20:00 report screenshot and a hand-check table for the same day.
Reliability proof: an error alert from conversation 15, the uptime monitor alert from a stopped-n8n test, and the GitHub commit containing the bot.
Cost sheet: tokens per message, AI cost per order, monthly executions and server vs. n8n Cloud comparison with price sources and dates.
A demo video of about 3 minutes: message, summary, Confirm, Orders row, evening report.
mistakes: Letting the AI return prices or totals and using them, so the injection test (conversation 8) changes what the customer is charged.
Creating the Orders row when the summary is sent instead of on the Confirm tap, or not checking the Pending status, so double taps create two orders.
Debugging with "Listen for test event" on the live bot, which steals its webhook and leaves real customers unanswered.
Building two workflows with Telegram Triggers for the same bot, so one of them never receives updates.
Leaving voice notes, photos or AI failures with no reply, when the brief says customers always get an answer.
Submitting cost and Cloud comparisons as guesses, without counted executions, measured tokens or dated price sources.

B4.intro: Use this guide to score Sage Desk against the 100-point rubric. Each row says what full, partial and low marks look like, so learners can check their own build before submitting and reviewers can score it consistently. A submission wins at 80 or more, and only if every critical evaluation case passes, whatever the total.

rows.full: The latest evaluation run shows 90% or more on 25+ cases. Every policy answer names its section and quotes money rules word for word (conversation 5 quotes the current late-delivery rule: after Curveball 1, the delivery fee plus 10% of the goods). Prices and order details match the sheets exactly, including the two-product total in conversation 2.
rows.partial: Accuracy between about 75% and 89%, or answers are right but some policy replies paraphrase money rules or don't name the section. One price or total is off in the 15 conversations.
rows.low: Under 75%, or the agent invents prices, policies or order details; no evidence of the evaluation run.

rows.full: Every critical and attack case passes. Conversation 7 shows no issue_refund call; conversation 4 refuses B access to A's order with nothing leaked; the card number in conversation 10 is masked before memory. Refunds reach Paystack test mode only after Tolu's Telegram approval, and the refund sub-workflow's code checks (owner, paid, not refunded, ≤ total, ≤ ₦50,000) are visible and tested.
rows.partial: Approval and limits are in place but one non-critical attack gets through to the reviewer or the output check, or one code limit is missing. No money moves without approval and no data leaks.
rows.low: Any critical case fails, money can move without approval, the agent supplies the customer's identity to a tool, or one customer can see another's data. A low score here means the boss is not won, whatever the total.

rows.full: Postgres memory keyed by tg-{chat_id}, window 8; conversation 11 keeps the address; "same as last time" reads the last order and asks to confirm; the 30-day clean-up runs. Conversation 12 sends Tolu a three-line summary (who, wants, tried), tells the customer when to expect a reply based on the hour, and the agent stops replying until Tolu releases it.
rows.partial: Memory works but the clean-up or the same-name test is missing, or the hand-over alerts Tolu without a useful summary, a time promise, or a pause.
rows.low: Memory is shared or keyed by name, conversations forget details within a few messages, or there's no working hand-over.

rows.full: An automated n8n Evaluations harness with 25+ cases (8+ critical, 5+ attacks) written before the agent, at least two versions compared run by run, and a two-page quality report that a non-technical reader understands: scope, test set, results by version, attacks, cost, monitoring and known limits.
rows.partial: Tests exist but are scored partly by hand, or only one version was run, or the report is accurate but too technical or missing a section.
rows.low: Fewer than 25 cases, no automated scoring, no report, or results claimed without screenshots or exported runs.

rows.full: Error workflow, uptime monitor and nightly backups cover Sage Desk; conversation 15 (provider down) gets a polite holding reply and an alert; Max Iterations is 6; cost per conversation is measured from real evaluation runs with a monthly estimate and a routing comparison.
rows.partial: Monitoring and alerts exist but backups or the provider-down test are missing, or cost is estimated without measured token counts.
rows.low: No error handling, the customer gets nothing when the provider fails, or no cost figure at all.

rows.full: All three handled with evidence: old policy chunks deleted by version inside the load workflow plus a "10%" test case; a language rule agreed with Tolu plus Yorùbá and Pidgin test cases checked by a fluent speaker; grouped hand-overs that send Tolu one summary when the same issue spikes.
rows.partial: Two of three handled, or all three described but only partly built or tested.
rows.low: One or none handled, or answers are ideas with no change to the build or tests.

rows.full: A video of about 4 minutes showing all five moments: a policy answer with the section named, an order lookup, a refund approved on Tolu's phone and the test refund recorded, an attack refused, and a hand-over with its summary.
rows.partial: Three or four of the five moments, or the video runs well over time and is hard to follow.
rows.low: No video, or fewer than three moments shown.

evidence: Exported n8n workflows (main agent, sub-workflows, load policies, clean-up, hand-over, error workflow) with credentials removed.
The evaluation sheet or data table with 25+ cases and the outputs of at least two runs, plus a screenshot of the Evaluations tab comparing runs.
A table of the 15 test conversations from two Telegram accounts, with a screenshot for each and pass or fail.
Screenshots of the approval message on Tolu's phone, the refund sub-workflow's code limits, and the Paystack test-mode refund reference.
The Decisions log and the Supabase memory table showing separate keys for accounts A and B (no real customer data).
Evidence for each curveball: the updated load workflow and test case, the language rule and new cases, and the grouped hand-over design.
The two-page quality report with cost per conversation and a monthly estimate.
A demo video of about 4 minutes covering the five moments.
mistakes: Shipping on a high average while one or more critical cases still fail.
get_order or issue_refund takes the customer or order owner from the model instead of the trigger, so account B can reach A's order.
The refund can reach Paystack by a path that skips Tolu's review, or live keys were used instead of test mode.
The evaluation set was written after the agent and only covers friendly questions, with too few attacks or "I don't know" cases.
The policy was reloaded without deleting old chunks, so the agent still quotes the previous rule.
Hand-over alerts Tolu but doesn't pause the agent or tell the customer when to expect a reply.

B5.intro: Use this guide after you have built Growth Desk and logged the 18 tests, or when reviewing someone else's. Score each rubric area against the evidence, not the description: a rule only counts if a test, log or screenshot shows it working. A win needs 80 points or more and every must-have in the go-live check passing; one missing must-have fails the build whatever the score.

rows.full: Places API plus websites only, place IDs stored rather than Places data; facts verified in code with a general line when none is found (test 1); every draft approved on Telegram; at most 20 sends a day from the outreach subdomain; suppression checked before every send and STOP never followed up (test 2); replies sorted by type.
rows.partial: The pipeline works but one safeguard is weak: the cap is not enforced in code, facts are not checked against the page, or replies are not sorted.
rows.low: Scraped or bought leads, sends without approval, the main domain used, or a STOP reply followed up.

rows.full: Two or more sources plus web mentions, deduplicated by item ID; four labels with agreement measured against a people-labelled set; food safety alerts on a hard rule within 15 minutes even at low confidence (test 7); a Monday report with code-counted numbers and three quoted fixes.
rows.partial: Labels and alerts work but agreement was never measured, or only one source is connected, or the report is AI-counted.
rows.low: Alerts on every negative label, the food-safety test missed, or commenter profiles stored.

rows.full: Calendar from real products and photos; versions for three or more platforms that pass each platform's checks (Instagram blocked without media, test 11); Telegram approval; prices re-read at publish time and a changed price held (test 10); pause switch; post IDs saved.
rows.partial: Two platforms only, or one check missing (price re-check or media check), or no pause switch.
rows.low: One caption for every platform, posts without approval, or prices taken from the draft.

rows.full: Meta webhooks plus at least one more channel in one queue; allowed actions computed in code (tests 3 to 6 pass); identities normalised, merged only on verified proof and never on names (tests 8 and 9); one answer on the latest channel; leads saved with source and consent; complaints handed to a named person with timers that alert.
rows.partial: Most tests pass but one rule is left to the agent's judgement, or leads lack a consent flag, or timers exist without alerts.
rows.low: Replies outside a messaging window, merges on a name, personal details in public replies, or several answers to one customer.

rows.full: Gmail Show original shows SPF, DKIM and DMARC as PASS; consent captured at checkout and recorded; welcome, weekly newsletter and 60-day win-back running; unapproved discounts blocked (test 12); unsubscribes stop marketing on every channel the same day (test 13); sends pause above 0.1% complaints (test 14).
rows.partial: Domain passes and sequences run, but unsubscribes only stop email, or one sequence is missing, or the complaint pause is manual.
rows.low: Free Gmail From address, a list without recorded consent, or failing authentication.

rows.full: GD·08 upserts every business lead by email and domain with associations and CRM IDs stored (test 16); a stage change creates one task and runs once (test 17); score calibrated on past leads; Ops Agent proposes only and nothing changes until Tolu approves (test 18); events trace a lead to first order (test 15); the Monday report shows cost per lead and per new customer, including Tolu's time, with a data-backed recommendation.
rows.partial: The CRM fills itself but cost per customer leaves out unbilled costs, or the score is not calibrated, or one sync test fails once.
rows.low: Leads typed by hand, duplicates or loops, an agent that writes to the CRM, or no source-to-customer tracing.

rows.full: A channel-rules sheet with a checked date per platform; a consent policy; monthly budgets for Places and X with alerts at 80%; pause switches for posting, outreach and campaigns; every go-live must-have ticked with evidence.
rows.partial: Rules sheet present but undated, or budgets set without alerts, or one pause switch missing.
rows.low: No rules sheet or budgets, or any must-have missing.

rows.full: All three answered with the system's real switches and numbers: pause and one approved statement for the viral video; an assisted Instagram mode plus a resubmission plan; cost per customer for outreach and Instagram from events, including Tolu's time.
rows.partial: Two handled well, or all three answered in general terms without the system's own numbers.
rows.low: One or none handled.

evidence: D1 growth plan: ICP, brand voice, consent policy, response targets, and the dated channel-rules sheet with API budgets and 80% alerts.
D2 data model: Supabase schema export (customers, identities, conversations, leads, posts, mentions, decisions, suppression, events).
Exported workflows for every engine (GD·01 to GD·08) with credentials removed, plus the error workflow and watchdog.
The 18-test log: expected, actual, execution ID and screenshot for each, using test accounts and your own inboxes only.
Gmail Show original screenshot with SPF, DKIM and DMARC PASS, and the CRM pipeline and dashboard screenshots.
The D7 growth report from a Monday run: leads and customers by source, weighted forecast, response times, cost per lead and per customer, complaints and unsubscribes, one recommendation.
The completed go-live check and compliance checklist, and written answers to the three curveballs.
A 4-minute demo video: prospect approved, comment to lead, one answer across two channels, a newsletter, a lead arriving in the CRM by itself, and the growth report.
mistakes: A must-have fails (for example, the suppression list is not checked before follow-ups, or a reply goes out after a window closed), so the build cannot win whatever the points.
Tests run against real customers or real businesses instead of test accounts and your own inboxes.
Cost per customer counts only invoices and leaves out AI tokens and Tolu's approval time, or the numbers come from the AI instead of the events table.
Engines that do not write lead_id or order_id events, so source to customer cannot be traced.
The CRM sync creates duplicates or loops, or the Ops Agent or a workflow changes deal stages.
Evidence is a description of what should happen, with no execution logs or screenshots.
